zh: 操作的效果是：一段长度至少为 2 的同字符段 x 可以把右边紧挨着的字符改成 x，于是这段变长、继续向右蔓延；被改写的字符总是变成它左边某个成对段的字母。
顺序很关键：先让最靠右的可蔓延段把它右边全部改成自己的字母，再让左边的下一段蔓延，这样左边的段经过右边区域时面对的是一整片相同的其他字母，能再改一遍。所以一段能贡献的次数就是它右侧当前与它不同的字符个数。
从右往左按段处理，维护“从位置 p 到末尾已经全部是字母 tail”。遇到长度≥2 的段 [l,r]（字母 y）时：贡献为 (r,p) 之间原字符中不等于 y 的个数（用 26 个字母的前缀计数求），若 tail≠y 再加 n−p；然后令 p=l、tail=y。长度为 1 的段跳过。答案可达约 n²/4，用 64 位整数。
en: The operation means a run of at least two equal characters x can rewrite the character just to its right into x, so the run grows and keeps spreading right. A rewritten character always becomes the letter of some paired run to its left.

Order matters: first let the rightmost run that can spread rewrite everything to its right into its own letter, then let the next run to the left spread. That run then meets one solid block of a different letter on the right and can rewrite all of it again. So the number of operations a run contributes is the number of characters to its right that currently differ from it.

Process runs from right to left, keeping the fact that positions p..end are all the letter tail. For a run [l,r] of length at least 2 with letter y, add the number of original characters strictly between r and p that differ from y (using prefix counts of the 26 letters), plus n-p if tail differs from y; then set p=l and tail=y. Skip runs of length 1. The answer can reach about n^2/4, so use 64-bit integers.

explanationEn:
## Problem

For a string s, one operation chooses three consecutive characters s[i], s[i+1], s[i+2]; when s[i]=s[i+1] and s[i+1]≠s[i+2], change s[i+2] into s[i]. Find the maximum number of operations that can be performed.

## Approach

The effect of an operation is that a run of identical characters x of length >=2 can "spread" to the right, changing the character immediately to its right into x, so the run keeps getting longer and keeps moving right. When it meets a character that is already x, it simply passes over it (the character merges into the run). So the number of operations a run of x can contribute is the number of characters to its right that are currently not x.

The key is the order: first let the rightmost run that can spread change everything to its right into its own character, then let the next run to the left spread. This way, when the run on the left passes over the region on the right, it faces another letter that is entirely uniform there, and it can rewrite it once more. Process the runs from right to left, maintaining that "from position p to the end everything is the character tail". When processing a run [l,r] of length >=2 (character y), its contribution is the number of original characters between (r,p) that are ≠y (computed with prefix counts of the 26 letters), plus n-p if tail≠y; then set p=l and tail=y. A run of length 1 cannot spread and stays as it is.

## Correctness

Only runs of identical characters with length >=2 can trigger an operation, and the character written is the character of that run, so every operation changes some position into the character of the adjacent run on its left. Each time a position is changed, a paired run different from it must spread over it from the left. The right-to-left order lets each position be changed once by every paired run on its left that differs from its current value, which is the maximum possible number. The implementation was also verified on small data with an exhaustive state search.

## Complexity

O(26n) time and space. The answer can reach about n^2/4, so use 64-bit integers.

## Independent verification

On small and medium data the oracle simulates step by step "always perform the rightmost feasible operation" until no operation is possible; on even smaller data, memoized search enumerates all operation orders and takes the maximum, proving that this simulation is optimal. All strings of length 1..8 over the alphabet {a,b,c} were enumerated exhaustively; all three agree, and the reference program was actually run on each one. The wrong solutions cover operating only once per run, not distinguishing characters that are already the same, 32-bit counting, and a single left-to-right scan.
